case_notes:
Provisional diagnosis: myeloid neoplasm, unspecified.

72F with persistent macrocytic anaemia. Bone marrow is reported as showing insufficient dysplastic change for a diagnosis of MDS. Blasts are not increased. Iron stain shows 7% ring sideroblasts.

NGS (myeloid panel):
- SF3B1 pathogenic variant, VAF 30%

No other case facts relevant to classifier-specific exclusions are supplied.

structured_case.detected_variants_summary: NGS detected an SF3B1 pathogenic variant (VAF 30%).

case_facts.value: Bone marrow has insufficient dysplastic change for a diagnosis of MDS; blasts are not increased.

It intentionally does not encode transcript, exon, or amplicon numbers.

## Negative-result semantics

When the patient NGS result is explicitly complete, a listed panel gene that is absent from the detected-variant list is interpreted as **no SNV, short insertion/deletion, or short-range complex variant detected in that gene within the validated assay scope**.

Use this negative result when applying diagnostic, prognostic, biomarker, treatment, germline, and other reporting rules. Do not treat the gene as unresolved merely because it is not individually listed in the patient result.

This inference is limited to the assay scope. It does not establish whole-gene biological wild type and does not exclude copy-number changes, rearrangements, structural variants, or other variant classes unless the patient result or another supplied test explicitly assesses them.

If the patient NGS result is described as partial, selected, limited, abbreviated, pending, or otherwise incomplete, do not infer a negative result for an unlisted panel gene.

diagnosis_evidence_cards.interpretation: According to the ICC, accelerated-phase CML is defined by any of the following: 10%-19% blasts in peripheral blood or bone marrow; peripheral-blood basophils >=20%; or a major-route additional clonal cytogenetic abnormality in Philadelphia-positive cells at diagnosis or acquired during treatment (second Philadelphia chromosome, trisomy 8, i(17q), trisomy 19, complex karyotype, or 3q26.2 abnormality).
According to the ICC, blast-phase CML is defined by >=20% blasts in peripheral blood or bone marrow or by myeloid sarcoma (extramedullary blast proliferation).
In CML, morphologically apparent lymphoblasts >5% warrant consideration of lymphoblastic crisis; immunophenotypic analysis is required to confirm lymphoid lineage.

According to the ICC, polycythemia vera requires either all 3 major criteria or the first 2 major criteria plus the minor criterion. Major criteria are: elevated hemoglobin (>16.5 g/dL in men or >16.0 g/dL in women), elevated hematocrit (>49% in men or >48% in women), or red-cell mass >25% above predicted; JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutation; and age-adjusted hypercellular marrow with trilineage proliferation (panmyelosis). The minor criterion is a subnormal serum erythropoietin level.

In patients with sustained absolute erythrocytosis (hemoglobin >18.5 g/dL in men or >16.5 g/dL in women and hematocrit >55.5% in men or >49.5% in women) plus JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutation, a bone marrow biopsy may not be required for polycythemia vera diagnosis.
In JAK2 exon 12-mutated polycythemia vera with isolated erythrocytosis and erythroid-predominant marrow, the usual panmyelosis diagnostic criterion may not apply.

According to the ICC, post-polycythemia vera myelofibrosis requires both required criteria—previous established polycythemia vera and bone-marrow fibrosis grade 2 or 3—plus at least 2 additional criteria: anemia or sustained loss of requirement for phlebotomy/cytoreductive treatment for erythrocytosis; leukoerythroblastosis; increased or newly palpable splenomegaly; or development of at least 2 of >10% weight loss in 6 months, night sweats, and unexplained fever >37.5°C.

According to the ICC, essential thrombocythemia requires all 4 major criteria or the first 3 major criteria plus the minor criterion. Major criteria are platelet count >=450 x 10^9/L; characteristic megakaryocytic-lineage proliferation with enlarged mature hyperlobulated megakaryocytes and no significant granulocytic/erythroid proliferation or relevant fibrosis; exclusion of BCR::ABL1-positive CML, polycythemia vera, primary myelofibrosis, and other myeloid neoplasms; and JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation. The minor criterion is another clonal marker or absence of reactive thrombocytosis.
Small dense megakaryocyte clusters can occur infrequently in essential thrombocythemia and therefore do not by themselves exclude that diagnosis.

According to the ICC, post-essential thrombocythemia myelofibrosis requires both required criteria—previous established essential thrombocythemia and bone-marrow fibrosis grade 2 or 3—plus at least 2 additional criteria: anemia with a >2 g/dL decrease from baseline hemoglobin; leukoerythroblastosis; increased or newly palpable splenomegaly; elevated LDH; or development of at least 2 of >10% weight loss in 6 months, night sweats, and unexplained fever >37.5°C.

According to the ICC, pre-fibrotic/early primary myelofibrosis requires all 3 major criteria and at least 1 minor criterion confirmed on 2 consecutive determinations. Major criteria are characteristic megakaryocytic proliferation/atypia with marrow fibrosis <grade 2, increased age-adjusted cellularity, granulocytic proliferation and often decreased erythropoiesis; JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation, another clonal marker, or absence of reactive reticulin fibrosis; and exclusion of BCR::ABL1-positive CML, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, MDS, and other myeloid neoplasms. Minor criteria are unexplained anemia, leukocytosis >=11 x 10^9/L, palpable splenomegaly, or elevated LDH.

According to the ICC, overt primary myelofibrosis requires all 3 major criteria and at least 1 minor criterion confirmed on 2 consecutive determinations. Major criteria are megakaryocytic proliferation/atypia with reticulin and/or collagen fibrosis grade 2 or 3; JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation, another clonal marker, or absence of reactive myelofibrosis; and exclusion of essential thrombocythemia, polycythemia vera, BCR::ABL1-positive CML, MDS, and other myeloid neoplasms. Minor criteria are unexplained anemia, leukocytosis >=11 x 10^9/L, palpable splenomegaly, elevated LDH, or leukoerythroblastosis.
In suspected primary myelofibrosis, detection of ASXL1, EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, or TET2 mutation can support the clonal nature of disease when canonical MPN-driver mutations are absent.
In primary myelofibrosis with monocytosis, a history of MPN excludes CMML, while a higher variant allele frequency of MPN-associated driver mutations supports PMF with monocytosis rather than CMML.

According to the ICC, chronic neutrophilic leukemia requires neutrophilic leukocytosis with segmented/band neutrophils >=80%, neutrophil precursors <10%, monocytes <10%, no significant dysgranulopoiesis, and hypercellular marrow with increased normally maturing neutrophil granulocytes; exclusion of BCR::ABL1-positive CML, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, primary myelofibrosis, and myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and TK fusions; and either CSF3R T618I/another activating CSF3R mutation or, if CSF3R is absent, persistent neutrophilia for >=3 months with splenomegaly and no reactive cause (with myeloid clonality demonstrated if a plasma-cell neoplasm is present). The WBC threshold is >=13 x 10^9/L with an activating CSF3R mutation and >=25 x 10^9/L without one; absence of CSF3R does not exclude CNL.
Significant monocytosis, basophilia, eosinophilia, or dysgranulopoiesis should prompt critical review of a proposed chronic neutrophilic leukemia diagnosis.
In chronic neutrophilic leukemia, 10%-19% blasts in peripheral blood or bone marrow represents accelerated phase, whereas >=20% blasts represents blast phase.

According to the ICC, chronic eosinophilic leukemia, NOS requires all 6 criteria: peripheral-blood eosinophils >=1.5 x 10^9/L and >=10% of leukocytes; <20% blasts in blood and marrow without another AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormality; absence of BCR::ABL1 and other ABL1, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2, or FLT3 TK fusions; failure to meet criteria for another well-defined MPN, CMML, or systemic mastocytosis; characteristic marrow abnormalities or increased blasts (>=5% marrow and/or >=2% blood); and a clonal cytogenetic abnormality and/or somatic mutation. If clonality or increased blasts are absent, supportive marrow findings can suffice when persistent eosinophilia is present and other causes are excluded.

According to the ICC, myeloproliferative neoplasm, unclassifiable (MPN-U) requires all 3 criteria: clinical and hematologic features of an MPN (with reactive causes excluded if marrow fibrosis is present); JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation or another clonal marker; and failure to meet criteria for another MPN, MDS, MDS/MPN, or BCR::ABL1-positive CML.

Myeloproliferative neoplasm, unclassifiable (MPN-U) is an appropriate ICC category for very early-phase MPN lacking fully developed subtype criteria or for splanchnic/portal-vein thrombosis with MPN features that do not meet a specific MPN subtype.
In myeloproliferative neoplasm, unclassifiable (MPN-U), ASXL1, EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, or TET2 mutations detected by sensitive molecular methods can support the clonal nature of disease.

diagnosis_evidence_cards.interpretation: When acute lymphoblastic leukemia carries a tyrosine-kinase fusion, involvement of background myeloid cells supports classification as myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusion rather than lymphoid-restricted BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL or de novo T-ALL.
The ICC classifies mastocytosis into cutaneous mastocytosis, generally skin-confined, and systemic mastocytosis, defined by extracutaneous involvement with or without skin disease.
The ICC recognizes five systemic mastocytosis subtypes: indolent, smoldering, aggressive, mast cell leukemia, and systemic mastocytosis with an associated myeloid neoplasm.

Bone-marrow mastocytosis is described as an indolent systemic mastocytosis variant characterized by limited bone-marrow infiltration, no skin lesions, and normal or slightly elevated serum tryptase levels.

According to the ICC, systemic mastocytosis is established by the major criterion—multifocal dense aggregates of >=15 tryptase- and/or CD117-positive mast cells in marrow and/or another extracutaneous organ—or, when the major criterion is absent, by at least 3 of 4 minor criteria: >25% spindle-shaped/atypical immature mast cells; mast-cell expression of CD25, CD2, and/or CD30; KIT D816V or another activating KIT mutation; and persistent serum tryptase >20 ng/mL (not counted in SM with an associated myeloid neoplasm). A TK fusion associated with myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia excludes systemic mastocytosis.

In systemic mastocytosis, mast cell leukemia is defined by atypical immature mast cells accounting for >=20% of bone marrow cellularity, with provision for diagnosis when the aspirate is a dry tap or otherwise suboptimal.
In systemic mastocytosis, the amount of circulating mast cells does not justify a separate leukemic versus aleukemic mast cell leukemia subcategory in the ICC.

Rare cases of systemic mastocytosis can show mature, round, well-granulated mast cells; these cases typically lack KIT D816V and are often CD25-negative, CD2-negative, and CD30-positive, with variable serum tryptase.

According to the ICC, systemic mastocytosis with an associated myeloid neoplasm requires meeting diagnostic criteria for systemic mastocytosis and for an associated myeloid neoplasm, with the associated neoplasm fully classified.

Monocytosis, eosinophilia, splenomegaly, elevated LDH, high KIT D816V variant allele frequency, and additional myeloid-malignancy mutations, particularly in combination, can raise suspicion for an associated myeloid neoplasm in systemic mastocytosis.

In rare systemic mastocytosis cases with both a KIT mutation and a myeloid/lymphoid-neoplasm tyrosine-kinase fusion, the ICC recommends assigning the fusion-defined myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm as the associated myeloid neoplasm only when both abnormalities are present.

According to the ICC, cytopenia together with cytosis is a key characteristic of MDS/MPN; cytopenia thresholds are hemoglobin <13 g/dL in males or <12 g/dL in females, ANC <1.8 x 10^9/L, or platelets <150 x 10^9/L.

According to the ICC, CMML requires persistent monocytosis (absolute monocytes >=0.5 x 10^9/L and >=10% of WBCs), cytopenia using MDS thresholds except that some early cases may have borderline/no cytopenia, <20% blasts including promonocytes in blood and marrow, marrow morphology consistent with CMML, and absence of BCR::ABL1 or TK-fusion myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms. Clonality is established by abnormal cytogenetics and/or a myeloid-neoplasm-associated mutation with allele frequency >=10%; without demonstrable clonality, monocytes must be >=1.0 x 10^9/L and >10% of WBCs together with increased blasts, morphologic dysplasia, or an abnormal CMML immunophenotype.

According to the ICC, CMML uses a 2-tier blast classification: CMML-1 has <5% blasts in peripheral blood and <10% in bone marrow; CMML-2 has 5%-19% blasts in blood, 10%-19% in marrow, or Auer rods. The former CMML-0 category is eliminated.
Development of an NPM1 mutation in established CMML should be noted but does not by itself define de novo AML.
The ICC myeloproliferative subtype of CMML (CMML-MP) is defined by WBC >13 x 10^9/L.

According to the ICC, atypical chronic myeloid leukemia (aCML) requires WBC >=13 x 10^9/L due to neutrophils and precursors with promyelocytes/myelocytes/metamyelocytes >=10%; cytopenia using MDS thresholds; <20% blasts; prominent dysgranulopoiesis; monocytes <10% and eosinophils <10% of leukocytes; hypercellular marrow with granulocytic proliferation/dysplasia; and absence of BCR::ABL1 and TK-fusion myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms. Absence of JAK2, CALR, and MPL supports the diagnosis, and SETBP1 mutation, often with ASXL1, provides additional support.
A history of MPN and/or JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation tends to exclude atypical chronic myeloid leukemia (aCML).
Detection of a CSF3R mutation in suspected atypical chronic myeloid leukemia (aCML) should prompt careful morphologic review to exclude chronic neutrophilic leukemia.

According to the ICC, MDS/MPN with SF3B1 mutation and thrombocytosis requires thrombocytosis >=450 x 10^9/L and anemia present at initial diagnosis, <1% blood blasts and <5% marrow blasts, and SF3B1 mutation with VAF >10%; no recent cytotoxic/growth-factor therapy explaining the phenotype; no prior MPN, MDS, or other MDS/MPN; and absence of BCR::ABL1, TK-fusion myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms, t(3;3), inv(3), and del(5q) meeting MDS-del(5q) criteria. Ring sideroblasts are not required when SF3B1 VAF is >10%; JAK2 V617F, CALR, or MPL W515 co-mutation is not required but supports the diagnosis.

According to the ICC, MDS/MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis, NOS requires thrombocytosis >=450 x 10^9/L and anemia present at initial diagnosis, erythroid dysplasia with >=15% ring sideroblasts, <1% blood blasts and <5% marrow blasts, and clonality by cytogenetic abnormality and/or somatic mutation (or, if clonality is absent, no recent cytotoxic/growth-factor therapy explaining the phenotype); no prior MPN, MDS, or other MDS/MPN; and absence of SF3B1 mutation, BCR::ABL1, TK-fusion myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms, t(3;3), inv(3), and del(5q) meeting MDS-del(5q) criteria.
MDS with SF3B1 mutation that later develops thrombocytosis is classified as thrombocytotic progression of MDS-SF3B1 rather than MDS/MPN with thrombocytosis.

According to the ICC, MDS/MPN NOS requires mixed myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative features that do not meet another MDS/MPN, MDS, or MPN category; cytopenia using MDS thresholds; <20% blasts in blood and marrow; platelets >=450 x 10^9/L and/or WBC >=13 x 10^9/L; evidence of clonality when demonstrable (or persistent findings with other causes excluded if clonality cannot be determined); and absence of BCR::ABL1, TK-fusion myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms, t(3;3), inv(3), and del(5q) meeting corresponding MDS criteria.
A history of MPN and/or JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation, particularly at high VAF, tends to exclude MDS/MPN NOS.
Hypereosinophilia in a case being considered as MDS/MPN NOS favors chronic eosinophilic leukemia, NOS instead.
The ICC MDS/MPN NOS category should not be used to classify advanced-stage MPN or triple-negative MPN merely because they are otherwise difficult to classify.

According to the ICC, MDS/MPN with i(17q) is a provisional subtype of MDS/MPN, NOS. Diagnosis requires leukocytosis >=13 x 10^9/L, cytopenia using MDS thresholds, <20% blasts in blood and bone marrow, dysgranulopoiesis with nonsegmented or pseudo-Pelger-Huet neutrophils, and i(17q) either isolated or with one additional abnormality other than -7/del(7q). BCR::ABL1, myeloid/lymphoid-neoplasm tyrosine-kinase gene fusions, and JAK2/CALR/MPL mutations should be absent, and recent cytotoxic or growth-factor therapy must not explain the phenotype. SRSF2 and SETBP1 co-mutations further support the diagnosis.

For clonal cytopenias spanning CCUS to MDS, the ICC defines cytopenia as acquired sustained hemoglobin <12 g/dL in females or <13 g/dL in males, ANC <1.8 x 10^9/L, and/or platelets <150 x 10^9/L not explained by another condition.
VEXAS syndrome is associated with somatic UBA1 mutation and should be kept separate from MDS unless morphologic MDS criteria are met.

According to the ICC, MDS is a clonal hematopoietic neoplasm defined by persistent unexplained cytopenia and morphologic dysplasia, generally chronic for about >=4 months and not explained by drug, toxin, or comorbidity; a 10% dysplasia threshold is recommended for each lineage, and demonstrable clonality is not required when qualifying dysplasia and cytopenia are present. BCR::ABL1 or a TK-fusion myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm excludes MDS. At initial diagnosis, persistent WBC >=13 x 10^9/L, platelets >=450 x 10^9/L (except MDS-del(5q) or inv(3)/t(3;3)), or monocytes >=0.5 x 10^9/L and >=10% of leukocytes instead favors MDS/MPN or MPN classification.

According to the ICC, MDS with mutated SF3B1 requires SF3B1 mutation VAF >=10%, at least one cytopenia, no ICC-defined cytosis at diagnosis, <5% marrow blasts and <2% blood blasts, and absence of multihit TP53, RUNX1 mutation, isolated del(5q), -7/del(7q), 3q26.2 abnormalities, and complex karyotype. Dysplasia is typically present but is not required, and ring sideroblasts are not required.
SF3B1-unmutated MDS with ring sideroblasts is classified as MDS, NOS irrespective of ring-sideroblast number.
In cytopenic patients lacking dysplasia, prior MDS-defining cytogenetic abnormalities other than del(5q), -7/del(7q), or complex karyotype are now classified as CCUS rather than MDS.

According to the ICC, MDS with excess blasts requires at least one cytopenia, no ICC-defined cytosis, and 5%-9% marrow blasts or 2%-9% blood blasts; 1% peripheral-blood blasts confirmed on two occasions also qualifies. Dysplasia is typically present but not required, multihit TP53 is excluded in favor of MDS with mutated TP53, and excess blasts supersede other non-TP53 MDS subtypes. In patients <18 years, MDS with excess blasts uses 5%-19% marrow blasts and 2%-19% blood blasts, and MDS/AML does not apply.

According to the ICC, MDS with del(5q) requires at least one cytopenia, del(5q) isolated or with no more than one additional cytogenetic abnormality other than -7/del(7q), <5% marrow blasts and <2% blood blasts, and absence of multihit TP53. Thrombocytosis is allowed but other ICC-defined cytoses are not; dysplasia is typically present but is not required.

According to the ICC, MDS, NOS without dysplasia requires at least one cytopenia, no ICC-defined cytosis, <5% marrow blasts and <2% blood blasts, and -7/del(7q) or complex karyotype as the defining cytogenetic abnormality; multihit TP53 and SF3B1 mutation with VAF >=10% are excluded.

According to the ICC, MDS, NOS with single-lineage dysplasia requires dysplasia in one lineage, at least one cytopenia, no ICC-defined cytosis, <5% marrow blasts and <2% blood blasts, and failure to meet criteria for MDS with del(5q) or MDS with mutated SF3B1; multihit TP53 is excluded.

According to the ICC, MDS, NOS with multilineage dysplasia requires dysplasia in at least two lineages, at least one cytopenia, no ICC-defined cytosis, <5% marrow blasts and <2% blood blasts, and failure to meet criteria for MDS with del(5q) or MDS with mutated SF3B1; multihit TP53 is excluded.

According to the ICC, adult MDS/AML is defined by 10%-19% blasts in blood or marrow, at least one cytopenia, and absence of ICC-defined cytosis. Generic MDS/AML excludes AML-defining cytogenetic abnormalities and NPM1, in-frame bZIP CEBPA, and TP53 mutations that define other genetic categories; dysplasia is typically present but not required. MDS/AML is subclassified as TP53-mutated, myelodysplasia-related gene-mutated, myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic, or NOS.

According to the ICC, MDS with mutated TP53 has 0%-9% blasts and requires multihit TP53, defined as 2 distinct TP53 mutations each with VAF >10% or one TP53 mutation plus 17p deletion, VAF >50%, or copy-neutral LOH at TP53; when LOH information is unavailable, TP53 mutation VAF >10% with complex karyotype qualifies. Complex karyotype without a TP53 mutation does not qualify, and monoallelic TP53-mutated MDS is excluded from this entity.
MDS/AML with mutated TP53 is defined by 10%-19% blasts and any somatic TP53 mutation with VAF >10%; monoallelic TP53 mutations are allowed.
AML with mutated TP53 is defined by >=20% marrow or blood blasts, or pure erythroid leukemia, plus any somatic TP53 mutation with VAF >10%; monoallelic TP53 mutations are allowed.
Established MDS that acquires a TP53 mutation can be redesignated as MDS, MDS/AML, or AML with mutated TP53 according to blast count.

Development of leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, or monocytosis during established MDS generally does not warrant reclassification as MDS/MPN; the disease can instead be designated as MDS with neutrophilic, thrombocytotic, or monocytic progression.
The ICC recommends retaining the morphologic/genetic MDS diagnosis as primary and adding a therapy-related qualifier when disease follows cytotoxic therapy.
The ICC recommends qualifying CHIP, CCUS, and other non-MDS clonal cytopenias as therapy-related when they follow marrow exposure to chemotherapy or radiation.
Any underlying germline predisposition mutation or syndrome should be specified as a qualifier after the MDS diagnosis and subtype.

According to the ICC, JMML is a RAS-pathway-defined neoplasm involving PTPN11, NRAS, KRAS, RRAS, NF1, or CBL and generally requires peripheral-blood monocytes >=1 x 10^9/L, splenomegaly, <20% blasts in blood and marrow, and absence of BCR::ABL1. One diagnostic genetic route is a somatic PTPN11, KRAS, NRAS, or RRAS mutation after excluding relevant germline Noonan-syndrome forms; the paper notes that a minority of JMML cases may present below the monocytosis threshold or without splenomegaly.

According to the ICC, JMML-like neoplasm is a clonal disorder phenotypically resembling JMML but lacking a canonical PTPN11, NRAS, KRAS, RRAS, NF1, or CBL RAS-pathway mutation; rare examples include ALK or ROS1 rearrangements and FIP1L1::RARA or CCDC88C::FLT3 fusions. AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormalities and myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and TK fusions are excluded.
In germline RUNX1-, ANKRD26-, or ETV6-associated constitutional platelet disorders, marrow megakaryocytic dysplasia can be present with isolated thrombocytopenia in the absence of MDS.
When assessing MDS in patients with germline predisposition, baseline dyspoietic bone-marrow changes can be present even in the absence of a myeloid malignancy.

In patients with germline predisposition, development of MDS is generally associated with new or progressive cytopenia, often with rising marrow cellularity, overt multilineage dysplasia, increased blasts, and/or acquired pathogenic genetic abnormalities.
In a patient with germline predisposition, emergence of del(5q), -7/del(7q), complex karyotype, multihit TP53 mutation VAF >10%, or SF3B1 mutation VAF >10% is considered MDS-defining.
In Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, a small stable clone with monoallelic TP53 mutation alone is not considered MDS, whereas biallelic TP53 mutation is associated with myeloid malignancy.
According to the ICC, acute promyelocytic leukemia with PML::RARA can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts.
According to the ICC, APL with other RARA rearrangements can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts; listed RARA partners include IRF2BP2, NPM1, ZBTB16, STAT5B, STAT3, TBL1XR1, FIP1L1, and BCOR.
According to the ICC, AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1, CBFB::MYH11, MLLT3::KMT2A, or DEK::NUP214 can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts.
According to the ICC, AML with other KMT2A rearrangements can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts; listed partners include AFF1, AFDN, MLLT10, TET1, ELL, and MLLT1.
According to the ICC, AML with inv(3) or t(3;3) involving GATA2 and MECOM can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts.
According to the ICC, AML with other MECOM rearrangements can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts; listed examples include MECOM rearrangements involving MYC, ETV6, or RUNX1.
According to the ICC, AML with BCR::ABL1 requires >=20% blasts.
The ICC does not use the MDS/AML category for BCR::ABL1-positive AML because of overlap with progression of BCR::ABL1-positive CML.
According to the ICC, AML with mutated NPM1 can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts.
According to the ICC, AML with an in-frame bZIP CEBPA mutation can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts, without requiring biallelic CEBPA mutations.
According to the ICC, MDS/AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations has 10%-19% blasts and is defined by mutation in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2.
According to the ICC, AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations requires >=20% blasts and is defined by mutation in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2.

After excluding TP53 mutation, myelodysplasia-related gene mutation, and other class-defining recurring genetic abnormalities, MDS/AML with myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities is defined at 10%-19% blasts by specified abnormalities including complex karyotype, del/t/add(5q), -7/del(7q), +8, del/t/add(12p), i(17q), -17/add(17p)/del(17p), del(20q), or idic(X)(q13).

After excluding TP53 mutation, myelodysplasia-related gene mutation, and other class-defining recurring genetic abnormalities, AML with myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities is defined at >=20% blasts by specified abnormalities including complex karyotype, del/t/add(5q), -7/del(7q), +8, del/t/add(12p), i(17q), -17/add(17p)/del(17p), del(20q), or idic(X)(q13).
AML, NOS requires >=20% blasts after excluding class-defining genetic categories.
MDS/AML, NOS applies at 10%-19% blasts after excluding the other defined MDS/AML genetic categories.
Myeloid sarcoma remains an ICC AML-related disease category and does not require a marrow or blood blast-percentage threshold for its classification.

For AML categories with listed recurrent genetic abnormalities other than BCR::ABL1 and the remaining >=20%-blast categories, the ICC permits AML diagnosis with at least 10% blasts or blast equivalents.
Single-gene mutation or gene-fusion AML categories take precedence over myelodysplasia-related gene-mutation and myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic groups.
When TP53 mutation overlaps another AML genetic category, the ICC states that the TP53 mutation should be noted with the other genetic abnormality.
Pure erythroid leukemia is typically TP53-mutated and is classified within AML with TP53 mutation in the ICC.
According to the ICC, therapy-related status is a diagnostic qualifier appended to the specific AML or MDS/AML diagnosis rather than a stand-alone AML disease category.
According to the ICC, progression from a confirmed prior MDS is a diagnostic qualifier appended to the specific AML or MDS/AML diagnosis.
According to the ICC, progression from a confirmed prior MDS/MPN is a diagnostic qualifier appended to the specific AML or MDS/AML diagnosis, with the antecedent MDS/MPN specified.
Underlying germline predisposition is used as a qualifier following the specific AML or MDS/AML diagnosis.

For TP53-mutated MDS, a single TP53 mutation with a retained wild-type copy represents a monoallelic state, whereas multiple TP53 mutations or TP53 mutation(s) with TP53 deletion or copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity represent multi-hit TP53, consistent with biallelic targeting.
diagnosis_evidence_cards.paper_nickname: Bernard TP53 Allelic State in MDS 2020

diagnosis_evidence_cards.interpretation: Under the 2022 International Consensus Classification (ICC), PML::RARA, RUNX1::RUNX1T1, CBFB::MYH11, MLLT3::KMT2A, DEK::NUP214, inv(3)/t(3;3) involving GATA2 and MECOM, mutated NPM1, and in-frame bZIP CEBPA mutations are AML-defining recurrent abnormalities at ≥10% blasts; BCR::ABL1 requires ≥20% blasts because of overlap with chronic myeloid leukemia.

Under the 2022 ICC, IRF2BP2::RARA, NPM1::RARA, ZBTB16::RARA, STAT5B::RARA, STAT3::RARA, TBL1XR1::RARA, FIP1L1::RARA, and BCOR::RARA are recognized recurring RARA-rearranged APL entities and, as AML-defining recurrent abnormalities other than BCR::ABL1, establish AML/APL at ≥10% blasts.
Under the 2022 ICC, AFF1::KMT2A, AFDN::KMT2A, MLLT10::KMT2A, TET1::KMT2A, KMT2A::ELL, and KMT2A::MLLT1 are recognized recurring KMT2A-rearranged AML entities and establish AML at ≥10% blasts.
Under the 2022 ICC, t(2;3) involving MECOM, MYC/MECOM t(3;8), ETV6::MECOM, and MECOM::RUNX1 are recognized recurring MECOM-rearranged AML entities and establish AML at ≥10% blasts.

Under the 2022 ICC, PRDM16::RPN1, RBM15::MRTFA, NPM1::MLF1, NUP98::NSD1, ETV6::MNX1, KAT6A::CREBBP, PICALM::MLLT10, NUP98::KMD5A, FUS::ERG, RUNX1::CBFA2T3, CBFA2T3::GLIS2, and other NUP98 rearrangements are listed as rare recurring AML-defining genetic entities and establish AML at ≥10% blasts.

Under the 2022 ICC, when higher-priority recurrent AML-defining abnormalities are absent, a pathogenic somatic TP53 mutation with variant allele fraction ≥10%, with or without loss of the wild-type allele, defines TP53-mutated AML at ≥20% blasts; the corresponding 10%-19% blast category is MDS/AML.

Under the 2022 ICC, when higher-priority recurrent AML-defining abnormalities and TP53-mutated disease are absent, pathogenic mutations in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2 define AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations at ≥20% blasts, irrespective of prior MDS; the corresponding 10%-19% blast category is MDS/AML.

Under the 2022 ICC, when higher-priority AML-defining categories are absent, del(5q)/t(5q)/add(5q), monosomy 7/del(7q), trisomy 8, del(12p)/t(12p)/add(12p), i(17q), monosomy 17/add(17p)/del(17p), del(20q), idic(X)(q13), or a complex karyotype of ≥3 unrelated chromosome abnormalities (excluding hyperdiploid karyotypes with ≥3 trisomies/polysomies and no structural abnormality) defines AML with myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormality at ≥20% blasts and MDS/AML at 10%-19% blasts.

Under the 2022 ICC, prior chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or immune intervention for a nonmyeloid neoplasm is recorded as a therapy-related diagnostic qualifier to the genetically defined AML category rather than as a separate AML entity.
Under the 2022 ICC, a prior MDS is appended as a diagnostic qualifier to the AML category only when it was established by standard diagnostics more than 3 months before AML diagnosis.

Under the 2022 ICC, the AML classification hierarchy is: recurrent AML-defining genetic abnormality first; otherwise TP53-mutated AML; otherwise AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations; otherwise AML with myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities.
Under the 2022 ICC, for a patient with a prior MDS/MPN such as CMML, the MDS/MPN diagnosis is retained until blasts or blast equivalents reach ≥20%.
Under the 2022 ICC, the former AML with myelodysplasia-related changes (AML-MRC) category is removed, and multilineage dysplasia is no longer an independent criterion for that AML category.

Under the 2022 ICC, cases lacking a recurrent AML-defining abnormality, TP53-mutated category, myelodysplasia-related gene mutation category, or myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic category are classified as AML, not otherwise specified at ≥20% blasts, or MDS/AML at 10%-19% blasts, irrespective of multilineage dysplasia.
Under the 2022 ICC, when an inherited germline predisposing disorder is identified in a patient with AML, the germline disorder is appended as a diagnostic qualifier to the specific AML category.
Under the 2022 ICC, BCR::ABL1-positive disease with 10%-19% blasts is classified as chronic myeloid leukemia in accelerated phase rather than AML.

Under the 2022 ICC, in a patient with a history of chronic myeloid leukemia, BCR::ABL1-positive disease with ≥20% blasts is classified as CML in myeloid blast phase rather than de novo AML with BCR::ABL1.

Under the 2022 ICC, a prior MDS/MPN is appended as a diagnostic qualifier to the AML category only when the MDS/MPN was established by standard diagnostics more than 3 months before AML diagnosis, and the MDS/MPN type should be specified.

Under the 2022 ICC, patients with a prior myeloproliferative neoplasm are excluded from the AML hierarchy and are classified as accelerated-phase MPN at 10%-19% blasts or MPN blast phase at ≥20% blasts.
Under the 2022 ICC, myeloblasts, monoblasts, and megakaryoblasts are included in the blast count used for AML classification.
Under the 2022 ICC, in AML with monocytic or myelomonocytic differentiation, monoblasts and promonocytes are counted as blast equivalents, whereas abnormal monocytes are not.
Under the 2022 ICC, in PML::RARA or variant RARA-rearranged APL/AML, promyelocytes are counted as blast equivalents for classification.

According to the FAB classification, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia is classified as myelodysplastic CMML when the leukocyte count is ≤13 × 10^9/L and myeloproliferative CMML when it is >13 × 10^9/L.
According to the 2016 WHO revision, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia includes dysplastic and proliferative types.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, cytopenia thresholds harmonized across CCUS, MDS and MDS/MPN are haemoglobin <13 g/dL in males or <12 g/dL in females, absolute neutrophil count <1.8 × 10^9/L, and platelets <150 × 10^9/L.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, chronic myeloid leukaemia is defined by BCR::ABL1 resulting from t(9;22)(q34;q11).

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, CML is classified into chronic and blast phases; accelerated phase is omitted. Blast phase is defined by ≥20% myeloid blasts in blood or bone marrow, extramedullary proliferation of blasts, or increased lymphoblasts in blood or marrow. The optimal lymphoblast cutoff and significance of low-level B-lymphoblasts remain uncertain.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, major diagnostic criteria for polycythaemia vera include elevated haemoglobin and/or haematocrit, bone-marrow trilineage hyperplasia (panmyelosis) with pleomorphic mature megakaryocytes, and JAK2 p.V617F or a JAK2 exon 12 mutation. Measurement of increased red-cell mass with 51Cr-labelled red cells is no longer a diagnostic criterion.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, recognition of prefibrotic primary myelofibrosis remains necessary to distinguish it from essential thrombocythaemia, polycythaemia vera and fibrotic primary myelofibrosis.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, chronic neutrophilic leukaemia is a BCR::ABL1-negative MPN characterized by sustained peripheral-blood neutrophilia with WBC ≥25 × 10^9/L and ≥80% segmented neutrophils and bands, bone-marrow hypercellularity due to neutrophilic granulocyte proliferation, and hepatosplenomegaly.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, chronic eosinophilic leukaemia is defined by sustained clonal proliferation of morphologically abnormal eosinophils and eosinophil precursors producing persistent hypereosinophilia in blood and marrow. Sustained hypereosinophilia requires ≥4 weeks; both clonality and abnormal bone-marrow morphology are required; increased blasts no longer substitute for clonality; and the former “not otherwise specified” qualifier is omitted.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MPN-U (MPN-NOS) is reserved for cases with clinical, laboratory, morphologic and molecular features of MPN that either fail criteria for a specific MPN type or overlap distinct MPN types.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, JMML diagnosis integrates clinical, laboratory and molecular criteria. Updated criteria exclude KMT2A rearrangements, no longer use monosomy 7 as a cytogenetic diagnostic criterion, and emphasize molecular studies demonstrating RAS-pathway activation.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, revised minor diagnostic criteria for systemic mastocytosis include any KIT mutation causing ligand-independent activation, CD30 expression, and basal serum tryptase >20 ng/mL; the tryptase value should be adjusted in hereditary alpha-tryptasaemia.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, KIT p.D816V with VAF ≥10% in bone-marrow cells or peripheral-blood leukocytes qualifies as a B-finding in systemic mastocytosis.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, bone marrow mastocytosis is a systemic mastocytosis subtype characterized by absence of skin lesions and B-findings and basal serum tryptase <125 ng/mL.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, the term “myelodysplastic neoplasms,” abbreviated MDS, replaces “myelodysplastic syndromes.” MDS is defined as a clonal haematopoietic neoplasm with cytopenia(s) and morphologic dysplasia, with a recommended dysplasia threshold of ≥10% in a lineage.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS with low blasts and isolated 5q deletion requires <5% bone-marrow blasts and <2% peripheral-blood blasts, with 5q deletion alone or with one additional abnormality other than monosomy 7 or 7q deletion. An SF3B1 mutation or a TP53 mutation that is not multi-hit does not by itself override the MDS-5q diagnosis.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS with low blasts and SF3B1 mutation is a genetically defined MDS type in which 5q deletion, monosomy 7 and complex karyotype are exclusionary. Detection of ≥15% ring sideroblasts may substitute for an SF3B1 mutation; for SF3B1-wild-type cases with ≥15% ring sideroblasts, “MDS with low blasts and ring sideroblasts” is an acceptable alternative term.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation requires <20% blasts in blood and marrow plus either ≥2 TP53 mutations or one TP53 mutation with TP53 copy-number loss or copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity. Two or more TP53 mutations can generally be considered multi-hit status. MDS-biTP53 supersedes MDS-5q and MDS-SF3B1 in the WHO5 genetic hierarchy.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, hypoplastic MDS is a distinct MDS type defined by bone-marrow cellularity ≤25%, adjusted for age.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, distinction between single-lineage and multilineage dysplasia is optional rather than disease-type defining in MDS.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, a 20% blast cutoff is retained to delineate MDS from AML, but most AML types with defining genetic abnormalities may be diagnosed below 20% blasts. AML with BCR::ABL1 and AML with CEBPA mutation remain exceptions requiring ≥20% blasts. When a genetically defined AML is diagnosed below 20%, morphologic and molecular findings must be correlated to establish that the defining abnormality is driving the disease.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, childhood MDS with low blasts replaces the former term refractory cytopenia of childhood and is defined by <5% bone-marrow blasts and <2% peripheral-blood blasts. It comprises hypocellular and NOS subtypes, and diagnosis requires exclusion of non-neoplastic causes of cytopenia, bone-marrow failure syndromes and germline pathogenic variants.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, childhood MDS with increased blasts is defined by 5–19% bone-marrow blasts or 2–19% peripheral-blood blasts.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, CMML requires all four prerequisite criteria: persistent absolute peripheral-blood monocytosis ≥0.5 × 10^9/L and relative monocytosis ≥10%; <20% blasts/blast equivalents in blood and marrow; absence of diagnostic criteria for CML or another MPN; and absence of a myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with a tyrosine-kinase fusion. Supporting criteria are dysplasia in ≥1 myeloid lineage, with ≥10% of cells affected; an acquired clonal cytogenetic or molecular abnormality; and abnormal monocyte partitioning with >94% classical monocytes in the absence of active autoimmune/systemic inflammatory disease. With monocytosis ≥1 × 10^9/L, at least one supporting criterion is required; with monocytosis ≥0.5 but <1 × 10^9/L, both dysplasia and clonality are required. A prior MPN excludes CMML; MPN-type marrow features and/or a high burden of JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations support MPN with monocytosis rather than CMML.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, CMML is subtyped as myelodysplastic CMML when WBC <13 × 10^9/L and myeloproliferative CMML when WBC ≥13 × 10^9/L. Blast-based subgrouping comprises CMML-1 with <5% blasts/promonocytes in blood and <10% in marrow and CMML-2 with 5–19% in blood and 10–19% in marrow; CMML-0 is no longer recognized.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, atypical chronic myeloid leukaemia is renamed MDS/MPN with neutrophilia.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS/MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis is redefined on the basis of SF3B1 mutation and renamed MDS/MPN with SF3B1 mutation and thrombocytosis. For SF3B1-wild-type cases with ≥15% ring sideroblasts, MDS/MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis remains acceptable terminology.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML is organized into two families: AML with defining genetic abnormalities and AML defined by differentiation. The term AML, NOS is no longer applied to the differentiation-defined family.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with PML::RARA, RUNX1::RUNX1T1, CBFB::MYH11, DEK::NUP214 or RBM15::MRTFA is classified as AML with a defining genetic abnormality.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with BCR::ABL1 requires ≥20% blasts, principally to avoid overlap with CML.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with CEBPA mutation includes either biallelic CEBPA mutations or a single CEBPA mutation in the basic leucine zipper region and requires ≥20% blasts.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with KMT2A, MECOM or NUP98 rearrangement may be diagnosed with <20% blasts.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with NPM1 mutation may be diagnosed irrespective of blast count, with judicious clinicopathologic correlation.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, somatic RUNX1 mutation does not define a standalone AML type because it lacks sufficient specificity across defining molecular contexts.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML, myelodysplasia-related (AML-MR; formerly AML with myelodysplasia-related changes) requires ≥20% blasts with a myeloid immunophenotype plus at least one qualifying MDS-related feature: a history of MDS or MDS/MPN; a defining somatic mutation in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1 or ZRSR2; or a defining cytogenetic abnormality comprising complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities), 5q deletion/loss, monosomy 7 or 7q deletion/loss, 11q deletion, 12p deletion/loss, monosomy 13 or 13q deletion, 17p deletion/loss, isochromosome 17q or idic(X)(q13). Morphologic dysplasia alone is insufficient. A diagnosis of acute erythroid leukaemia supersedes AML-MR.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with minimal differentiation requires blasts negative (<3%) for MPO and SBB by cytochemistry and expression of at least two myeloid-associated antigens such as CD13, CD33 and CD117. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML without maturation requires ≥3% blasts positive for MPO or SBB, NSE negativity, <10% maturing granulocytic cells and expression of at least two myeloid-associated antigens. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with maturation requires ≥3% blasts positive for MPO or SBB, ≥10% maturing granulocytic cells, <20% monocyte-lineage cells and expression of at least two myeloid-associated antigens. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, acute basophilic leukaemia requires basophilic blasts/immature or mature basophils with metachromasia on toluidine blue, blasts negative for MPO, SBB and NSE, and absence of strong CD117-equivalent expression. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, acute myelomonocytic leukaemia requires ≥20% monocytes and precursors, ≥20% maturing granulocytic cells and ≥3% blasts positive for MPO. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, acute monocytic leukaemia requires ≥80% monocytes and/or their precursors, <20% maturing granulocytic cells, and blasts/promonocytes expressing at least two monocytic markers among CD11c, CD14, CD36 and CD64 or showing NSE positivity. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, acute erythroid leukaemia is characterized by erythroid predominance, usually ≥80% of marrow cellularity, with ≥30% proerythroblasts; cases with <80% erythroid cellularity are recognized when they share the same clinicopathologic features. “Pure erythroid leukaemia” is retained as an acceptable related term. The other shared differentiation-defined AML exclusions apply, but the ≥20% blast requirement does not.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia requires blasts expressing at least one platelet glycoprotein marker—CD41, CD61 or CD42b. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with other defined genetic alterations provides a classification category for uncommon or emerging genetically defined AML subtypes, including rare genetic fusions; CBFA2T3::GLIS2 is recognized in this category in the acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia context.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, a myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy (MN-pCT) is diagnosed when criteria for AML, MDS or MDS/MPN are fulfilled in a patient with a documented history of chemotherapy or large-field radiation therapy for an unrelated neoplasm. CCUS is excluded. NPM1-mutated disease and core-binding-factor leukaemias with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 or CBFB::MYH11 still receive the post-cytotoxic designation when the exposure history is present. PARP1 inhibitors qualify as an exposure and methotrexate does not. The specific myeloid diagnosis should be given when possible with “post cytotoxic therapy” appended.

diseases: myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and TK fusion
diagnosis_evidence_cards.interpretation: According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) are BCR::ABL1-negative neoplasms driven by defining tyrosine-kinase rearrangements; eosinophilia is common but is not required. Defining abnormalities include rearrangements of PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2 or FLT3; ETV6::ABL1; and other defined fusions including ETV6::FGFR2, ETV6::LYN, ETV6::NTRK3, RANBP2::ALK, BCR::RET and FGFR1OP::RET. MLN-TK supersedes other myeloid or lymphoid diagnoses and systemic mastocytosis in the diagnostic hierarchy, must be excluded before diagnosing CEL, and MLN-TK with ETV6::ABL1 should be distinguished from B-ALL with ETV6::ABL1.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia is categorized under myeloproliferative neoplasms.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS with low blasts is defined by <5% bone-marrow blasts and <2% peripheral-blood blasts.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS with increased blasts is subgrouped as MDS-IB1, defined by 5–9% bone-marrow blasts or 2–4% peripheral-blood blasts, and MDS-IB2, defined by 10–19% bone-marrow blasts, 5–19% peripheral-blood blasts, or Auer rods.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS with fibrosis has 5–19% bone-marrow blasts and 2–19% peripheral-blood blasts.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS, unclassifiable is no longer a recognized MDS category.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS/MPN, unclassifiable is renamed MDS/MPN, not otherwise specified.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, “AML with KMT2A rearrangement” replaces the former term “AML with t(9;11)(p22;q23); KMT2A-MLLT3.”
In unexplained cytopenia, SF3B1 mutation strongly supports an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype, including when SF3B1 is the only detected mutation.
In unexplained cytopenia, SRSF2, U2AF1, ZRSR2, JAK2, or RUNX1 mutation strongly supports an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype, whether detected alone or with other mutations.

In unexplained cytopenia, an isolated TET2, DNMT3A, or ASXL1 mutation provides substantially less support for an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype, than the same mutation occurring with additional genetic lesions.
In unexplained cytopenia, TP53 mutation is more supportive of an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype, when co-mutated—most often with TET2 or ASXL1—than when TP53 is isolated.

In unexplained cytopenia, co-mutation patterns in which TET2, DNMT3A, or ASXL1 co-occurs with RUNX1, EZH2, CBL, TP53, NRAS, CUX1, or IDH2 are highly predictive of an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype.

In unexplained cytopenia, SF3B1 mutation is highly specific for a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia—MDS, MDS/MPN, or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes—even when SF3B1 is the only detected mutation.
In unexplained cytopenia, ZRSR2 mutation is highly specific for a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia—MDS, MDS/MPN, or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes.

In unexplained cytopenia, co-mutation patterns in which TET2, ASXL1, or DNMT3A co-occurs with RUNX1, EZH2, CBL, BCOR, CUX1, TP53, IDH1, or IDH2 are highly specific for a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia—MDS, MDS/MPN, or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes.

In unexplained cytopenia, SRSF2 or U2AF1 mutation is highly specific for a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia—MDS, MDS/MPN, or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes—except when co-occurring with JAK2 in primary myelofibrosis.

In patients with CCUS and inconclusive dysplasia, the authors propose that highly specific mutation patterns—SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2 mutation, or TET2, ASXL1, or DNMT3A co-mutated with RUNX1, EZH2, CBL, BCOR, CUX1, TP53, IDH1, or IDH2—may provide presumptive evidence of MDS even when definitive morphologic criteria are absent.
In MDS with del(5q), del(5q) can be the sole founding and disease-defining genetic lesion; an accompanying sequence mutation is not required.

In TP53-mutated AML/MDS, findings supporting multihit TP53 status include TP53 cnLOH demonstrated by dedicated testing; loss of chromosome 17 or 17p; two or more TP53 mutations; or a single TP53 mutation with VAF >55% and sequencing coverage >200×. A TP53 VAF <55% does not exclude multihit disease.

In TP53-mutated AML/MDS, complex karyotype may suggest multihit TP53 status but is an imperfect surrogate: some TP53-mutated cases with complex karyotype lack chromosome 17 deletion or TP53 cnLOH, whereas some cases with TP53 cnLOH have noncomplex karyotypes.

According to WHO 2022 as summarized by Urrutia et al., MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation has <20% blasts and no history of cytotoxic or radiation therapy; biallelic TP53 inactivation is defined by two or more TP53 mutations, one TP53 mutation with chromosome 17/17p copy loss, or one TP53 mutation with TP53 cnLOH.
